bw: Enzyme made by JG cells of the afferent arteriole
tp: Renin release is stimulated by prostaglandins and NO from the JGA when extracellular fluid volume falls.

ww.Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE): ACE makes angiotensin II from angiotensin I.
ww.Aldosterone: Aldosterone is an adrenal cortex steroid.

evidence: Renin is an enzyme that is produced by the juxtaglomerular (JG) cells of the afferent arteriole at the JGA.

bw: Made in the lungs but binds afferent arteriole and glomerular endothelium
tp: ACE converts inactive angiotensin I into active angiotensin II. ACE inhibitors are prescribed for high blood pressure.

ww.Renin: Renin is made by JG cells in the kidney.
ww.Angiotensin II: Angiotensin II is a hormone, the product of ACE.

evidence: ACE is not a hormone but it is functionally important in regulating systemic blood pressure and kidney function.

bw: Angiotensin II in blood loss or dehydration
ans: GFR and renal blood flow fall
d: GFR and renal blood flow rise
GFR rises while renal blood flow falls
tp: Angiotensin II constricts both afferent and efferent arterioles, limiting fluid loss and preserving blood volume.
evidence: In instances of blood loss or dehydration, it reduces both GFR and renal blood flow, thereby limiting fluid loss and preserving blood volume.

tp: Its release follows angiotensin II or directly follows raised plasma K+.

ww.Antidiuretic hormone: ADH comes from the posterior pituitary and conserves water.
ww.Atrial natriuretic hormone: ANH promotes sodium loss, the opposite of aldosterone.

evidence: Aldosterone, often called the “salt-retaining hormone,” is released from the adrenal cortex in response to angiotensin II or directly in response to increased plasma K+.

bw: Steroid that binds the aldosterone receptor
Water retention in some phases of the menstrual cycle
tp: It only weakly stimulates Na+ reabsorption and is unimportant in men because circulating levels are low.

ww.Testosterone: The source does not link testosterone to the aldosterone receptor.
ww.Oxytocin: Oxytocin is a peptide hormone and not a steroid.

evidence: It may cause increased retention of water during some periods of the menstrual cycle in women when progesterone levels increase.

bw: Often prescribed to lower blood pressure
tp: Diuretics interfere with the recapture of solutes and water from the forming urine. ADH does the opposite.

ww.Antidiuretics: These, like ADH, promote water recovery.
ww.Vasopressors: These raise blood pressure by vasoconstriction.

evidence: Diuretics are drugs that can increase water loss by interfering with the recapture of solutes and water from the forming urine.

bw: Chronically elevated in diabetic kidney disease
tp: Endothelins also lower GFR by damaging podocytes and constricting both afferent and efferent arterioles.
evidence: On the other hand, in people with diabetic kidney disease, endothelin is chronically elevated, resulting in sodium retention.

bw: Peptides that make the kidneys excrete sodium
tp: They inhibit aldosterone and ADH release, so both Na+ and water recovery fall.

ww.Mineralocorticoids: Mineralocorticoids such as aldosterone retain sodium.

evidence: Natriuretic hormones are peptides that stimulate the kidneys to excrete sodium—an effect opposite that of aldosterone.

bw: Afferent arteriole dilates and efferent arteriole constricts
tp: ANH is released when atrial stretch is high, as in high blood pressure or heart failure, and increases loss of water and sodium.

ww.GFR decreases: The arteriolar changes raise glomerular pressure.

evidence: It increases GFR through concurrent vasodilation of the afferent arteriole and vasoconstriction of the efferent arteriole.

bw: Diagnostic marker of congestive heart failure
tp: BNP has 10-fold lower receptor affinity than ANH, so it may serve as fine tuning for blood pressure.

ww.Atrial natriuretic hormone (ANH): ANH is made by the atria and has a shorter half-life.
ww.Antidiuretic hormone (ADH): ADH is a posterior pituitary hormone, not a cardiac natriuretic peptide.

evidence: BNP’s longer biologic half-life makes it a good diagnostic marker of congestive heart failure (Figure 25.21).

bw: Effect on phosphate in the PCT
tp: Losing phosphate in urine prevents calcium phosphate forming in plasma, so circulating calcium can be higher.

ww.Stimulates phosphate reabsorption: PTH causes phosphate to be lost in the urine.
ww.Has no effect on phosphate: The source lists blocking phosphate reabsorption as a PTH action.

evidence: It also blocks reabsorption of phosphate (PO3–), causing its loss in the urine.
